_note: The reference grammar: a machine-readable definition of the SysML v2 / KerML textual notation, derived clause by clause with traceable evidence. The Rust parser is checked against it; it is not generated from it.

AcceptNode@sysml.decision: A transcription of SysML 8.2.2.17.4. The clause and the Xtext state this production identically — `OccurrenceUsagePrefix AcceptNodeDeclaration ActionBody` in both (SysML.xtext:1442) — so there is nothing to weigh. All three parts are mandatory; the optionality lives one level down, in AcceptNodeDeclaration's `ActionNodeUsageDeclaration?`, which is what lets an accept node be written with or without the 'action' keyword and a name.

AcceptNodeDeclaration@sysml.decision: A transcription of SysML 8.2.2.17.4: `ActionNodeUsageDeclaration? 'accept' AcceptParameterPart`. The pinned pilot grammar states it identically at SysML.xtext:1446, as a fragment, which is an inlining mechanism of that parser generator rather than a claim about the language. Everything after the keyword is AcceptParameterPart, the same production a transition's TriggerAction reaches, which is what lets a trigger and an accept node share their payload and 'via' syntax while differing in what precedes them.

AcceptParameterPart@sysml.decision: A transcription of SysML 8.2.2.17.4. The clause and the Xtext state this production identically, so there is nothing to weigh. The payload is mandatory and the 'via' port is not, which is what makes `accept S` and `accept ignitionCmd:IgnitionCmd via ignitionCmdPort` the same production. It carries no 'accept' of its own: that keyword belongs to AcceptNodeDeclaration or to a transition's TriggerActionMember, which is how one production serves an accept node and a trigger alike.

ActionBehaviorMember@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.17.1 states ActionBehaviorMember : FeatureMembership = BehaviorUsageMember | ActionNodeMember. The SysML Xtext has no ActionBehaviorMember rule; it inlines the two alternatives into ActionBodyItem. The rule is the clause as written.

ActionBody@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.17.1 states ActionBody : Type = ';' | '{' ActionBodyItem* '}'. The SysML Xtext uses a `=>` syntactic predicate, which exists to steer the pilot's LL parser and is not ported. The rule is the clause as written.

ActionBodyItem@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.17.1 states ActionBodyItem : Type = NonBehaviorBodyItem | ownedRelationship += InitialNodeMember ( ownedRelationship += ActionTargetSuccessionMember )* | ( ownedRelationship += SourceSuccessionMember )? ownedRelationsuip += ActionBehaviorMember ( ownedRelationship += ActionTargetSuccessionMember )* | ownedRelationship += GuardedSuccessionMember. The SysML Xtext inlines NonBehaviorBodyItem's alternatives, names the optional leading member EmptySuccessionMember where the clause names SourceSuccessionMember, TargetSuccessionMember where it names ActionTargetSuccessionMember, and inlines ActionBehaviorMember as ( BehaviorUsageMember | ActionNodeMember ), and uses `=>` syntactic predicates; the inlining, the renamed productions and the predicates are not ported, since the clause names its own productions. `ownedRelationsuip` is a misspelt property in an assignment, not syntax. The rule is the clause as written.

ActionBodyParameter@sysml.decision: A transcription of SysML 8.2.2.17.7: `( 'action' UsageDeclaration? )? '{' ActionBodyItem* '}'`. The Xtext agrees on every token — its ActionUsageKeyword resolves through ActionKeyword to the single literal 'action' — with two things not carried over. `{SysML::ActionUsage}` is an object-creating action that consumes no input. The '=>' before `ActionBodyItem*` is a syntactic predicate, an LL workaround for a parser generator this project does not use, and porting it would make the grammar describe the pilot rather than the language. The braces are mandatory here, unlike an ActionBody, which is what makes a branch or loop body always a block and never a bare ';'.

ActionBodyParameterMember@sysml.decision: A transcription of SysML 8.2.2.17.7. The clause and the Xtext state this production identically — `ownedRelatedElement += ActionBodyParameter` in both — so there is nothing to weigh. It contributes no tokens; the braces of a branch or loop body belong to ActionBodyParameter below it. It is the member that puts a body in a parameter position, which is what makes the body of an if or a loop an argument of the node rather than a nested namespace.

ActionDefinition@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.17.1 states OccurrenceDefinitionPrefix 'action' 'def' DefinitionDeclaration ActionBody, and the SysML Xtext agrees (the same structure; the keyword pair is factored into a keyword rule, a renaming). The rule is the clause as written.

ActionNode@sysml.decision: A transcription of SysML 8.2.2.17.2. The clause and the Xtext offer the same eight alternatives and differ only in the order they are listed: the clause leads with ControlNode and the Xtext puts it last. Order between alternatives is not part of the language — it is a disambiguation strategy for a parser generator that tries them in sequence — and these eight are told apart by their leading keyword in any case, so nothing depends on it. The clause's order is kept, as the clause is the source. No alternative is added or dropped: ControlNode is the one that fans out to the merge, decide, fork and join nodes, which is why the list is eight long rather than eleven.

ActionNodeMember@sysml.decision: A transcription of SysML 8.2.2.17.1. The clause and the Xtext state this production identically — `MemberPrefix ownedRelatedElement += ActionNode` in both — so there is nothing to weigh. It is the membership wrapper that lets an action node appear as a member of an action body: the node's own syntax is entirely in ActionNode, and this rule adds only the MemberPrefix that every member may carry. It sits alongside ActionTargetSuccessionMember and GuardedSuccessionMember in the same clause, which have the same shape over their own element, so following the clause here also keeps the three consistent.

ActionNodePrefix@sysml.decision: A transcription of SysML 8.2.2.17.2. The clause and the Xtext state this production identically — `OccurrenceUsagePrefix ActionNodeUsageDeclaration?` in both — so there is nothing to weigh. Both parts can derive empty, so the prefix as a whole is optional in effect, which is why `if i < 0 {` needs nothing before the keyword. It is the shared head of the structured control nodes, where the node keyword follows it; the simpler control nodes use ControlNodePrefix instead, which is a different production.

ActionNodeUsageDeclaration@sysml.decision: A transcription of SysML 8.2.2.17.2: `'action' UsageDeclaration?`. The Xtext writes `ActionUsageKeyword UsageDeclaration?`, and ActionUsageKeyword (SysML.xtext:1403) is an alias for ActionKeyword (1349), which is the single literal 'action'. Two levels of alias over one keyword, so the two accept the same text and the clause's literal is written directly. The keyword is mandatory and the declaration is not, which is what makes a bare `action` legal as the head of a node that needs no name — and, since UsageDeclaration is itself nullable, the '?' here is belt and braces rather than a second reading.

ActionTargetSuccession@sysml.decision: A transcription of SysML 8.2.2.17.8. The clause and the Xtext state this production identically, token for token, so there is nothing to weigh: it is the choice of the three target-succession forms followed by a UsageBody. The three alternatives are distinguished by their leading token — 'then' for TargetSuccession, 'if' for the guarded form, 'else' for the default form — so the choice is decidable on one token and no ordering between them is implied. Factoring the shared UsageBody out of the three, as the clause does, is kept rather than distributed into each alternative.

ActionTargetSuccessionMember@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.17.1 states ActionTargetSuccessionMember : FeatureMembership = MemberPrefix ownedRelatedElement += ActionTargetSuccession. The SysML Xtext has no ActionTargetSuccessionMember rule; ActionBodyItem uses TargetSuccessionMember. The rule is the clause as written.

ActionUsage@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.17.2 states ActionUsage = OccurrenceUsagePrefix 'action' ActionUsageDeclaration ActionBody. The SysML Xtext factors the keyword into a keyword rule, a renaming. The rule is the clause as written.

ActionUsageDeclaration@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.17.2 states ActionUsageDeclaration : ActionUsage = UsageDeclaration ValuePart?. The SysML Xtext writes UsageDeclaration?; UsageDeclaration is Identification FeatureSpecializationPart?, whose Identification the specification makes nullable, so the '?' adds nothing. The rule is the clause as written.

ActorMember@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.21.1 states ActorMember : ActorMembership = MemberPrefix ownedRelatedElement += ActorUsage. The SysML Xtext is identical. The rule is the clause as written.

ActorUsage@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.21.1 states ActorUsage : PartUsage = 'actor' UsageExtensionKeyword* Usage. The SysML Xtext is identical. The rule is the clause as written.

AliasMember.decision: A member prefix, `alias`, an optional short name in angle brackets, an optional name, `for`, the qualified name being aliased, and a relationship body — exactly as KerML 8.2.3.4.1 states it. BOTH names are optional and independently so, which means `alias for X;` parses: an alias that names nothing. That is what the clause says, and it is not narrowed here.

AllocationDefinition@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.15 states OccurrenceDefinitionPrefix 'allocation' 'def' Definition, and the SysML Xtext agrees (the same structure; the keyword pair is factored into a keyword rule, a renaming). The rule is the clause as written.

AllocationUsage@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.15 states AllocationUsage = OccurrenceUsagePrefix AllocationUsageDeclaration UsageBody. The SysML Xtext is identical. The rule is the clause as written.

AllocationUsageDeclaration@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.15 states AllocationUsageDeclaration : AllocationUsage = 'allocation' UsageDeclaration ( 'allocate' ConnectorPart )? | 'allocate' ConnectorPart. The SysML Xtext writes UsageDeclaration? and factors the keywords into keyword rules; UsageDeclaration is already nullable, so neither changes the language. The rule is the clause as written.

AnalysisCaseDefinition@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.23 states OccurrenceDefinitionPrefix 'analysis' 'def' DefinitionDeclaration CaseBody, and the SysML Xtext agrees (the same structure; the keyword pair is factored into a keyword rule, a renaming). The rule is the clause as written.

AnalysisCaseUsage@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.23 states AnalysisCaseUsage = OccurrenceUsagePrefix 'analysis' ConstraintUsageDeclaration CaseBody. The SysML Xtext writes ActionUsageDeclaration where the clause writes ConstraintUsageDeclaration, and factors the keyword into a keyword rule; SysML 8.2.2.17.2 and 8.2.2.20 give both declarations the same body, UsageDeclaration ValuePart?, so neither difference changes the language. The rule is the clause as written.

AnnotatingElement@kerml.decision: KerML 8.2.3.3.1 states four alternatives, Comment | Documentation | TextualRepresentation | MetadataFeature, and the KerML Xtext states the same four in the same order. The rule is the clause as written.

AnnotatingElement@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.4.1 prints MetadataFeature as the fourth alternative, KerML's wording; the SysML Xtext writes MetadataUsage. That disagreement is already adjudicated and recorded as deviation AnnotatingElement (follow_xtext): SysML reads MetadataUsage, which its abstract syntax makes a MetadataFeature, so the printed alternative is satisfied rather than contradicted. The first three alternatives match the clause and the Xtext exactly.

AnnotatingMember@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.4.1 states AnnotatingMember : OwningMembership = ownedRelatedElement += AnnotatingElement; the SysML Xtext prefixes it with MemberPrefix. That disagreement is adjudicated and recorded as deviation AnnotatingMember (follow_xtext), on SYSML21-319, in which the specification's editor reports the missing MemberPrefix as a defect. The rule is MemberPrefix AnnotatingElement.

Annotation.decision: Both clauses state Annotation = annotatedElement = [QualifiedName], a cross-reference and nothing else, and the KerML Xtext agrees ([SysML::Element|QualifiedName]). A cross-reference [QualifiedName] is a ref to QualifiedName by the derivation's convention. The KerML and SysML texts are identical, so the unit is shared.

ArgumentExpressionValue.decision: `value = OwnedExpressionReference`. A reference, not an OwnedExpression: this is the one difference between an argument and an argument expression, and it is what makes the operand lazy.

ArgumentList.decision: Parentheses around an optional list, positional or named but not both. The optionality is what makes `f()` legal, and it is also why an empty pair of parentheses is ambiguous with NullExpression until the context is known.

ArgumentValue.decision: `value = OwnedExpression`. This is where an operand becomes any expression, and so where the expression grammar becomes recursive.

AssertConstraintUsage@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.20 states AssertConstraintUsage = OccurrenceUsagePrefix 'assert' ( isNegated ?= 'not' )? ( ownedRelationship += OwnedReferenceSubsetting FeatureSpecializationPart? | 'constraint' ConstraintUsageDeclaration ) CalculationBody. The SysML Xtext is the same, with 'constraint' as a keyword rule. The rule is the clause as written.

AssignmentNode@sysml.decision: A transcription of SysML 8.2.2.17.5. The clause and the Xtext state this production identically — `OccurrenceUsagePrefix AssignmentNodeDeclaration ActionBody` in both (SysML.xtext:1535) — so there is nothing to weigh. The shape is the same as AcceptNode's and, in the Xtext, SendNode's: a prefix, a declaration that carries the keyword and the operands, and a body. Everything optional is inside the declaration.

AssignmentNodeDeclaration@sysml.decision: A transcription of SysML 8.2.2.17.5. The clause and the Xtext state this production identically, token for token (SysML.xtext, declared a fragment, which is an inlining mechanism rather than a claim about the language). The target is split across two members on purpose: AssignmentTargetMember carries the optional prefix expression and its '.', and FeatureChainMember carries the feature being assigned, so `counter.count := 0` binds `counter` as the target's prefix and `count` as the chain. The ':=' is this production's own token and is not the FeatureValue ':=' of 8.2.2.6.2.

AssignmentTargetBinding@sysml.decision: A transcription of SysML 8.2.2.17.5: `ownedRelatedElement += NonFeatureChainPrimaryExpression`. It contributes no tokens of its own; the prefix expression it holds is written below it. The choice of NonFeatureChainPrimaryExpression rather than a general expression is the load-bearing part and is the clause's own: a feature chain is excluded here precisely because the '.' that would continue the chain belongs to AssignmentTargetParameter, so admitting one would make `counter.count` ambiguous between a chain and a prefix-plus-feature. There is no second opinion to weigh: the pinned pilot grammar has no rule of this name, reaching the same position through TargetBinding behind a '=>' syntactic predicate.

AssignmentTargetMember@sysml.decision: A transcription of SysML 8.2.2.17.5: `ownedRelatedElement += AssignmentTargetParameter`. The Xtext writes `ownedRelatedElement += TargetParameter`, which is not the same production under another name: its TargetParameter (SysML.xtext:1550) is `( => ownedRelationship += TargetBinding '.' )? ownedRelationship += TargetFeatureMember`, carrying the assigned feature inside itself, while the clause's AssignmentTargetParameter is `( ownedRelationship += AssignmentTargetBinding '.' )?` alone and AssignmentNodeDeclaration places the FeatureChainMember beside it. The two decompose the same tokens differently. The clause's decomposition is taken, consistently with AssignmentNodeDeclaration, which was derived from the same clause with FeatureChainMember as a sibling; taking the Xtext's here would state the feature twice. Its `=>` is a syntactic predicate in any case, an LL workaround that is not ported.

AssignmentTargetParameter@sysml.decision: A transcription of SysML 8.2.2.17.5: `( ownedRelationship += AssignmentTargetBinding '.' )?`. The whole production is optional, so it derives the empty string where an assignment names its target with no prefix. The '.' is part of this production rather than of the feature that follows, which is what splits `counter.count` into a target parameter `counter.` here and a FeatureChainMember `count` beside it in AssignmentNodeDeclaration. There is no second opinion to weigh: the pinned pilot grammar has no rule of this name, reaching the same tokens through TargetParameter, which folds in the assigned feature as well; that decomposition was declined on AssignmentTargetMember.

Association@kerml.decision: KerML 8.2.5.4 states Association = TypePrefix 'assoc' ClassifierDeclaration TypeBody. The KerML Xtext is identical. The rule is the clause as written.

AssociationStructure@kerml.decision: KerML 8.2.5.4 states AssociationStructure = TypePrefix 'assoc' 'struct' ClassifierDeclaration TypeBody. The KerML Xtext is identical. The rule is the clause as written.

AttributeDefinition@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.7 states AttributeDefinition : AttributeDefinition = DefinitionPrefix 'attribute' 'def' Definition, and the SysML Xtext agrees (the same structure; the keyword pair is factored into a keyword rule, a renaming). The rule is the clause as written.

AttributeUsage@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.7 states AttributeUsage : AttributeUsage = UsagePrefix 'attribute' Usage. The SysML Xtext factors the keyword into a keyword rule, a renaming. The rule is the clause as written.

BaseExpression.decision: Seven alternatives, in the clause's order. These are the expressions that are not built out of other expressions by an operator: a literal, a reference, an invocation, a constructor, a body, the null, or metadata access.

BasicDefinitionPrefix@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.6.1 states BasicDefinitionPrefix = isAbstract ?= 'abstract' | isVariation ?= 'variation'. The SysML Xtext is identical. The rule is the clause as written.

BasicFeaturePrefix@kerml.decision: An optional direction, then optional `derived`, `abstract`, `composite` or `portion`, and `var` or `const`, in that fixed order, as KerML 8.2.4.3.1 states it. Every part is optional, so the prefix can be empty.

BasicUsagePrefix@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.6.2 states BasicUsagePrefix : Usage = RefPrefix ( isReference ?= 'ref' )?, and the SysML Xtext fragment is identical. The corpus lines `ref controller : VehicleController;` and `ref part tlc = ...` open with the optional 'ref'. The rule is the clause as written.

Behavior@kerml.decision: KerML 8.2.5.6.1 states Behavior = TypePrefix 'behavior' ClassifierDeclaration TypeBody. The KerML Xtext is identical. The rule is the clause as written.

BehaviorUsageElement@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.6.4 states BehaviorUsageElement : Usage = ActionUsage | CalculationUsage | StateUsage | ConstraintUsage | RequirementUsage | ConcernUsage | CaseUsage | AnalysisCaseUsage | VerificationCaseUsage | UseCaseUsage | ViewpointUsage | PerformActionUsage | ExhibitStateUsage | IncludeUseCaseUsage | AssertConstraintUsage | SatisfyRequirementUsage. The SysML Xtext is identical. The rule is the clause as written.

BehaviorUsageMember@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.6.1 states BehaviorUsageMember : FeatureMembership = MemberPrefix ownedRelatedElement += BehaviorUsageElement. The SysML Xtext is identical. The rule is the clause as written.

BinaryConnectorDeclaration@kerml.decision: KerML 8.2.5.5.1 states BinaryConnectorDeclaration : Connector = ( FeatureDeclaration? 'from' | isSufficient ?= 'all' 'from'? )? ownedRelationship += ConnectorEndMember 'to' ownedRelationship += ConnectorEndMember. The KerML Xtext is identical. The rule is the clause as written.

BinaryConnectorPart@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.13.1 states BinaryConnectorPart : ConnectionUsage = ownedRelationship += ConnectorEndMember 'to' ownedRelationship += ConnectorEndMember. The SysML Xtext is the same syntax, returning SysML::Connector. The rule is the clause as written.

BinaryInterfacePart@sysml.decision: A transcription of SysML 8.2.2.14.2. The clause and the Xtext state this production identically. The Xtext writes it as a `fragment`, which is an Xtext inlining mechanism — a fragment is spliced into every rule that calls it rather than producing a parse node — and says nothing about the language; the specification names it as a production in its own right and InterfacePart selects between it and NaryInterfacePart, so it is kept as a production. Exactly two ends, joined by 'to': the n-ary form with three or more ends is NaryInterfacePart, which is bracketed and comma-separated and so cannot be confused with this one.

BinaryOperator.decision: Nineteen literals, in the clause's order. All map to DataFunctions in Table 5 and are evaluated eagerly, unlike ConditionalBinaryOperator's four.

BinaryOperatorExpression.decision: Both operands are ArgumentMembers, so both are evaluated. Contrast ConditionalBinaryOperatorExpression, whose right operand is referenced instead.

BindingConnector@kerml.decision: A feature prefix, `binding`, the declaration, and the body — four parts, exactly as KerML 8.2.5.5.2 states it, and the Xtext agrees. Everything that varies about a binding connector lives in BindingConnectorDeclaration and belongs to that unit.

BindingConnectorAsUsage@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.13.2 states BindingConnectorAsUsage = UsagePrefix ( 'binding' UsageDeclaration )? 'bind' ownedRelationship += ConnectorEndMember '=' ownedRelationship += ConnectorEndMember UsageBody. The SysML Xtext writes UsageDeclaration? inside the group and DefinitionBody in place of UsageBody; neither is ported, since the clause names its own productions. The rule is the clause as written.

BindingConnectorDeclaration@kerml.decision: As KerML 8.2.5.5.2 states it, with two alternatives. The first is a FeatureDeclaration, optionally followed by `of` end `=` end. The second is an optional `all`, then optionally the two ends, with `of` itself optional. The Xtext fragment is identical. The second alternative derives the empty string, so `binding;` alone is a BindingConnector. Where there is no FeatureDeclaration, `of` may be omitted, giving the common `binding a = b;`. No corpus file uses the empty form or `all`; those rest on the clause and the Xtext.

BodyExpression.decision: `ownedRelationship += ExpressionBodyMember`. Typed as a FeatureReferenceExpression: a body is referenced, not evaluated where it is written, which is what lets `select`, `collect` and `reduce` decide when to run it.

BooleanExpression@kerml.decision: A feature prefix, `bool`, an optional declaration, an optional value and a function body. The declaration is OPTIONAL: KERML11-181 names clause 8.2.5.7.4 and quotes this production, so the missing `?` is an acknowledged defect. Note that `bool` appears nowhere in the pinned corpus, so nothing here is corpus-confirmed and the citation is the only backstop.

BracketExpression.decision: The operand, then a bracketed sequence. The clause makes `[` the operator, so this is an OperatorExpression whose operator is a bracket rather than a word.

CalculationBody@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.19 states CalculationBody : Type = ';' | '{' CalculationBodyPart '}', and the SysML Xtext agrees (identical). The rule is the clause as written.

CalculationBodyItem@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.19 states CalculationBodyItem : Type = ActionBodyItem | ownedRelationship += ReturnParameterMember. The SysML Xtext is identical. The rule is the clause as written.

CalculationBodyPart@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.19 states CalculationBodyPart : Type = CalculationBodyItem* ( ownedRelationship += ResultExpressionMember )?. The SysML Xtext uses a `=>` syntactic predicate, which exists to steer the pilot's LL parser and is not ported. The rule is the clause as written.

CalculationDefinition@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.19 states OccurrenceDefinitionPrefix 'calc' 'def' DefinitionDeclaration CalculationBody, and the SysML Xtext agrees (the same structure; the keyword pair is factored into a keyword rule, a renaming). The rule is the clause as written.

CalculationUsage@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.19 states CalculationUsage = OccurrenceUsagePrefix 'calc' ActionUsageDeclaration CalculationBody. The SysML Xtext factors the keyword into a keyword rule, a renaming. The rule is the clause as written.

CaseBody@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.22 states CaseBody : Type = ';' | '{' CaseBodyItem* ( ownedRelationship += ResultExpressionMember )? '}'. The SysML Xtext uses a `=>` syntactic predicate, which exists to steer the pilot's LL parser and is not ported. The rule is the clause as written.

CaseBodyItem@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.22 states CaseBodyItem : Type = ActionBodyItem | SubjectMember | ActorMember | ObjectiveMember. Deviation CaseBodyItem (follow_xtext) adds ReturnParameterMember, which the SysML Xtext reaches through CalculationBodyItem and SysML 7.22-7.24 require. The rule names ReturnParameterMember directly rather than taking over the Xtext's CalculationBodyItem reference, which would say the same thing through another production.

CaseDefinition@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.22 states OccurrenceDefinitionPrefix 'case' 'def' DefinitionDeclaration CaseBody, and the SysML Xtext agrees (the same structure; the keyword pair is factored into a keyword rule, a renaming). The rule is the clause as written.

CaseUsage@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.22 states CaseUsage = OccurrenceUsagePrefix 'case' ConstraintUsageDeclaration CaseBody. The SysML Xtext writes ActionUsageDeclaration where the clause writes ConstraintUsageDeclaration, and factors the keyword into a keyword rule; SysML 8.2.2.17.2 and 8.2.2.20 give both declarations the same body, UsageDeclaration ValuePart?, so neither difference changes the language. The rule is the clause as written.

ChainingPart@kerml.decision: As KerML 8.2.4.3.1 states it: `chains`, then either an OwnedFeatureChaining or a FeatureChain. The Xtext fragment is identical. Neither alternative is defined in this clause, so whether they can overlap is for their own units to establish. FeatureDeclaration repeats FeatureRelationshipPart, so a feature may carry more than one ChainingPart, and the corpus has exactly that.

Class@kerml.decision: KerML 8.2.5.2 states Class = TypePrefix 'class' ClassifierDeclaration TypeBody. The KerML Xtext is identical. The rule is the clause as written.

ClassificationExpression.decision: The operand is optional, which is what lets `as Safety` and `@Safety` stand on their own after a dot or inside a filter, with the subject supplied by context. The test operators take a TypeReferenceMember and the cast takes a TypeResultMember: a test yields a boolean about the type, a cast yields the type, and the membership each builds is where that difference is recorded.

ClassificationTestOperator.decision: Three literals, in the clause's order. `@` is the classification test, distinct from `@@`, which is MetaclassificationTestOperator and tests the metaclass.

Classifier@kerml.decision: KerML 8.2.4.2.1 states Classifier = TypePrefix 'classifier' ClassifierDeclaration TypeBody. The KerML Xtext is identical. The rule is the clause as written.

ClassifierDeclaration@kerml.decision: KerML 8.2.4.2.1 states ClassifierDeclaration : Classifier = ( isSufficient ?= 'all' )? Identification ( ownedRelationship += OwnedMultiplicity )? ( SuperclassingPart | ConjugationPart )? TypeRelationshipPart*. The KerML Xtext writes Identification? where the clause writes Identification; the specification's Identification (KerML 8.2.3.1) is ( '<' NAME '>' )? NAME? and can already be empty, so the '?' adds nothing, and references its own ClassifierConjugationPart where the clause references ConjugationPart; that rule is not a specification production and its body is not in this pack, so the clause's reference is kept. The rule is the clause as written.

CollectExpression.decision: A dot followed by a body rather than a feature. The dot is shared with FeatureChainExpression, so which production applies turns on what follows it.

Comment.decision: As KerML 8.2.3.3.2 and SysML 8.2.2.4.2 both state it, so one shared unit. An optional `comment` header comes first: an Identification and an optional `about` list of Annotations. Then an optional `locale` string, then the REGULAR_COMMENT body. Everything before the body is optional, so a bare `/* ... */` is a Comment element in the model, not trivia. A parser and the oracle's lexer must deliver REGULAR_COMMENT as a token, not discard it. The Xtext writes `Identification?`, which is the same language, because the specification's Identification is nullable (KerML 8.2.3.1). The KerML clause misspells the first property `ownedRelationsip`, which consumes no tokens. KERML11-109 lists 'Relationsip' on page 79 without naming a production; whether that page holds this clause is not established here.

ConcernDefinition@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.21.3 states OccurrenceDefinitionPrefix 'concern' 'def' DefinitionDeclaration RequirementBody, and the SysML Xtext agrees (the same structure; the keyword pair is factored into a keyword rule, a renaming). The rule is the clause as written.

ConcernUsage@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.21.3 states ConcernUsage = OccurrenceUsagePrefix 'concern' ConstraintUsageDeclaration RequirementBody. The SysML Xtext factors the keyword into a keyword rule, a renaming. The rule is the clause as written.

ConditionalBinaryOperator.decision: Four literals, in the clause's order. These are the short-circuiting operators: Table 5 maps every one of them to a ControlFunctions function, which is what separates them from BinaryOperator's DataFunctions operators and why the specification gives them their own production and their own expression form.

ConditionalBinaryOperatorExpression.decision: Left operand is an ArgumentMember and right is an ArgumentExpressionMember. The asymmetry is the short-circuit: the right operand is referenced, not evaluated, which is exactly what separates this from BinaryOperatorExpression, where both sides are ArgumentMembers.

ConditionalExpression.decision: The ternary. Its condition is an ArgumentMember and both branches are ArgumentExpressionMembers, which is not decoration: an ArgumentExpression wraps its value in an OwnedExpressionReference, so the branches are referenced rather than evaluated in place. That is how a conditional evaluates only the branch it takes, and it is visible in the grammar rather than left to semantics.

ConjugatedPortDefinition@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.12 states ConjugatedPortDefinition = ownedRelationship += PortConjugation. The SysML Xtext is identical. The rule is the clause as written.

ConjugatedPortDefinitionMember@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.12 states ConjugatedPortDefinitionMember : OwningMembership = ownedRelatedElement += ConjugatedPortDefinition. The SysML Xtext is identical. The rule is the clause as written.

ConjugatedPortTyping@sysml.decision: As SysML 8.2.2.12 states it: `~` followed by `~[QualifiedName]`. Note 2 of the clause says that notation parses an ordinary QualifiedName from the text and changes only how it resolves: to the conjugated port definition named `'~C'` inside `A::B::C`. So syntactically it is `~` then a QualifiedName. The Xtext writes `conjugatedPortDefinition = [SysML::ConjugatedPortDefinition | ConjugatedQualifiedName]`, where its ConjugatedQualifiedName rule is `'~' QualifiedName`: the same tokens. The clause names the property `originalPortDefinition` and the Xtext `conjugatedPortDefinition`; a property name consumes no tokens.

Conjugation@kerml.decision: KerML 8.2.4.1.3 states Conjugation = ( 'conjugation' Identification )? 'conjugate' ( conjugatedType = [QualifiedName] | conjugatedType = FeatureChain ) CONJUGATES ( originalType = [QualifiedName] | originalType = FeatureChain ) RelationshipBody. The KerML Xtext writes `Identification?` inside the optional group and OwnedFeatureChain where the clause writes FeatureChain; neither is taken over, since the clause's own reference is FeatureChain. CONJUGATES is the special lexical terminal of KerML 8.2.2.7, '~' | 'conjugates'. The `{ ownedRelatedElement += ... }` actions are abstract syntax, not syntax. The rule is the clause as written.

ConjugationPart@kerml.decision: As KerML 8.2.4.1.1 states it: the CONJUGATES terminal followed by one OwnedConjugation. CONJUGATES is not a production. It is one of the special lexical terminals of KerML 8.2.2.7, `CONJUGATES = '~' | 'conjugates'`, which match either the symbol or the keyword, so the rule writes it out as that two-way choice. The Xtext fragment expands it the same way. Unlike SpecializationPart, which the same clause states just above, there is no comma-separated repetition: a type conjugates exactly one other type.

ConnectionDefinition@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.13.1 states OccurrenceDefinitionPrefix 'connection' 'def' Definition, and the SysML Xtext agrees (the same structure; the keyword pair is factored into a keyword rule, a renaming). The rule is the clause as written.

ConnectionUsage@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.13.1 states ConnectionUsage = OccurrenceUsagePrefix ( 'connection' UsageDeclaration ValuePart? ( 'connect' ConnectorPart )? | 'connect' ConnectorPart ) UsageBody. The SysML Xtext writes UsageDeclaration? and factors the keywords into keyword rules; UsageDeclaration is already nullable, so neither changes the language. The rule is the clause as written.

Connector@kerml.decision: A feature prefix, `connector`, then either a plain optional declaration with an optional value or a full connector declaration, then the body. Exactly as KerML 8.2.5.5.1 states it, and the Xtext agrees character for character.

ConnectorDeclaration@kerml.decision: As KerML 8.2.5.5.1 states it: a binary or an n-ary connector declaration. The Xtext fragment is identical. The same clause shows the two are separated after the optional FeatureDeclaration: a binary declaration continues with `from`, `all` or a connector end followed by `to`, and an n-ary one with `(`.

ConnectorEnd.decision: KerML 8.2.5.5.1 and SysML 8.2.2.13.1 state the same body: an optional OwnedCrossMultiplicityMember, an optional declaredName = NAME followed by REFERENCES, then OwnedReferenceSubsetting. They differ only in the result metaclass (Feature in KerML, ReferenceUsage in SysML), which is not syntax, so one shared rule serves both. REFERENCES is the special lexical terminal of KerML 8.2.2.7, written out as '::>' | 'references'. The Xtext's OwnedCrossingMultiplicityMember and ReferencesKeyword are renamings of the same pieces, not a different language.

ConnectorEndMember.decision: A membership wrapping one ConnectorEnd, with no tokens of its own. KerML 8.2.5.5.1 and SysML 8.2.2.13.1 state the same body, `ownedRelatedElement += ConnectorEnd`, so this is one shared unit. The SysML clause prints the header as `ConnectorEndMember : EndFeatureMembership :` with a colon where `=` belongs. The body after it is unambiguous and the rule is unaffected; whether OMG has filed this occurrence was not searched. ConnectorEnd itself differs between the languages (a Feature in KerML, a ReferenceUsage in SysML), and that belongs to ConnectorEnd's own unit or units. The Xtext rule agrees.

ConnectorPart@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.13.1 states ConnectorPart : ConnectionUsage = BinaryConnectorPart | NaryConnectorPart. The SysML Xtext is identical. The rule is the clause as written.

ConstraintDefinition@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.20 states OccurrenceDefinitionPrefix 'constraint' 'def' DefinitionDeclaration CalculationBody, and the SysML Xtext agrees (the same structure; the keyword pair is factored into a keyword rule, a renaming). The rule is the clause as written.

ConstraintUsage@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.20 states ConstraintUsage = OccurrenceUsagePrefix 'constraint' ConstraintUsageDeclaration CalculationBody. The SysML Xtext factors the keyword into a keyword rule, a renaming. The rule is the clause as written.

ConstraintUsageDeclaration@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.20 states ConstraintUsageDeclaration : ConstraintUsage = UsageDeclaration ValuePart?. The SysML Xtext writes UsageDeclaration?; UsageDeclaration is Identification FeatureSpecializationPart?, whose Identification the specification makes nullable, so the '?' adds nothing. The rule is the clause as written.

ConstructorExpression.decision: `new`, the type, then the constructor's result. The only difference from InvocationExpression is the keyword and that the arguments arrive through ConstructorResultMember rather than directly.

ConstructorResult.decision: A ConstructorResult is an ArgumentList: the arguments a constructor was given are its result's features.

ControlNode@sysml.decision: A transcription of SysML 8.2.2.17.3. The clause and the Xtext offer the same four alternatives in the same order, so there is nothing to weigh. Each is told apart by its own keyword — 'merge', 'decide', 'join', 'fork' — and the four share the identical shape below that (ControlNodePrefix, the keyword, a UsageDeclaration and an ActionBody), which is why the specification keeps them as four productions rather than one rule over a choice of keyword.

ControlNodePrefix@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.17.3 states this production, but prints `( isIndividual ?= 'individual )?` with no closing quote, so read literally the literal never terminates and no rule can be derived. The quote is closed: the intended literal is 'individual', which the attribute name isIndividual, the `?=` idiom and the pilot grammar all agree on, and which is the minimal repair. Recorded as the deviation ControlNodePrefix, follow_spec; the defect is filed as SYSML21-400, open. Otherwise the clause is transcribed: `isIndividual ?=` and the `{ isPortion = true }` beside PortionKind are assignments into the abstract syntax and contribute no tokens, so the rule carries the keyword and the kind alone.

Crosses.decision: As KerML 8.2.4.3.1 and SysML 8.2.2.6.5 both state it, so one shared unit: the CROSSES terminal, then exactly one OwnedCrossSubsetting. KerML 8.2.2.7 and SysML 8.2.2.1.2 define CROSSES identically, as `'=>' | 'crosses'`, and the rule writes it out as that choice. The Xtext calls a CrossesKeyword rule where the clauses name the terminal. The terminal is written out here.

DataType@kerml.decision: KerML 8.2.5.1 states DataType = TypePrefix 'datatype' ClassifierDeclaration TypeBody. The KerML Xtext is identical. The rule is the clause as written.

DecisionNode@sysml.decision: A transcription of SysML 8.2.2.17.3: `ControlNodePrefix isComposite ?= 'decide' UsageDeclaration ActionBody`. The `isComposite ?=` assigns into the abstract syntax and contributes no token. The Xtext's `UsageDeclaration?` against the clause's `UsageDeclaration` is redundant, not wider: UsageDeclaration is nullable through Identification (8.2.2.6.2 and 8.2.2.2), so both accept a decision node written with no name at all, which the corpus does. Same shape as MergeNode beside it; no deviation.

DefaultInterfaceEnd@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.14.1 states DefaultInterfaceEnd : PortUsage = isEnd ?= 'end' Usage. The SysML Xtext is identical. The rule is the clause as written.

DefaultReferenceUsage@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.6.3 states DefaultReferenceUsage : ReferenceUsage = RefPrefix Usage. Deviation DefaultReferenceUsage (follow_xtext) makes two changes, both the SysML Xtext's: an optional bare 'end', and a declaration that is not empty. By the clause's letter RefPrefix, UsageDeclaration (through a nullable Identification) and ValuePart can all be empty and UsageBody can be ';', so a lone ';' is a member. The Xtext's UsageDeclaration requires a name or a FeatureSpecializationPart. The rule writes Usage out as its declaration and UsageCompletion so the declaration can be required: a name, short and/or long, optionally specialized, or a FeatureSpecializationPart alone, as Identification (KerML 8.2.3.1) and UsageDeclaration (SysML 8.2.2.6.2) state them.

DefaultTargetSuccession@sysml.decision: A transcription of SysML 8.2.2.17.8. The Xtext accepts the same tokens and differs only by a leading `ownedRelationship += EmptyParameterMember`, which contributes none: a difference in the abstract syntax the pilot builds, not in the syntax it accepts, so the clause is followed. This is the same token-free member the Xtext also adds to GuardedTargetSuccession, and it is declined for the same reason. The production is the 'else' branch of a decision: no guard, no source, only the target, which is what distinguishes it from the guarded and plain forms it sits beside in the clause.

Definition@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.6.1 states Definition = DefinitionDeclaration DefinitionBody. The SysML Xtext is identical. The rule is the clause as written.

DefinitionBody@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.6.1 states DefinitionBody : Type = ';' | '{' DefinitionBodyItem* '}'. The SysML Xtext is identical. The rule is the clause as written.

DefinitionBodyItem@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.6.1 states DefinitionBodyItem : Type = ownedRelationship += DefinitionMember | ownedRelationship += VariantUsageMember | ownedRelationship += NonOccurrenceUsageMember | ( ownedRelationship += SourceSuccessionMember )? ownedRelationship += OccurrenceUsageMember | ownedRelationship += AliasMember | ownedRelationship += Import. The SysML Xtext writes the same alternatives, naming the optional leading member EmptySuccessionMember and putting a `=>` predicate on Import; the renaming and the predicate are not ported. The rule is the clause as written.

DefinitionDeclaration@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.6.1 states DefinitionDeclaration : Definition Identification SubclassificationPart?. The SysML Xtext writes Identification? SubclassificationPart?; whether the '?' on Identification changes the language depends on Identification's rule, which is not in this pack, so it is not read as a disagreement. The clause's header lacks its '=' (`DefinitionDeclaration : Definition` followed directly by the body); the body is unambiguous and is taken as written. The rule is the clause as written.

DefinitionElement@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.5.2 lists 29 alternatives; the SysML Xtext lists the same 29 plus AllocationDefinition. That disagreement is adjudicated and recorded as deviation DefinitionElement (follow_xtext): the clause omits AllocationDefinition editorially, leaving `allocation def` unreachable, and the corpus's Annex A model uses it as a package member. The rule is the clause's 29 alternatives plus AllocationDefinition and nothing else; the Xtext's different ordering is not ported because order does not change the language.

DefinitionExtensionKeyword@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.6.1 states DefinitionExtensionKeyword : Definition = ownedRelationship += PrefixMetadataMember. The SysML Xtext is identical. The rule is the clause as written.

DefinitionMember@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.6.1 states DefinitionMember : OwningMembership = MemberPrefix ownedRelatedElement += DefinitionElement. The SysML Xtext is identical. The rule is the clause as written.

DefinitionPrefix@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.6.1 states DefinitionPrefix : Definition = BasicDefinitionPrefix? DefinitionExtensionKeyword*. The SysML Xtext is identical. The rule is the clause as written.

Dependency@kerml.decision: KerML 8.2.3.2 states Dependency = ( ownedRelationship += PrefixMetadataAnnotation )* 'dependency' ( Identification? 'from' )? client += [QualifiedName] ( ',' client += [QualifiedName] )* 'to' supplier += [QualifiedName] ( ',' supplier += [QualifiedName] )* RelationshipBody. The KerML Xtext is identical apart from typing the cross-references as [SysML::Element|QualifiedName]. The rule is the clause as written.

Dependency@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.3 states Dependency = ( ownedRelationship += PrefixMetadataAnnotation )* 'dependency' DependencyDeclaration RelationshipBody, and the SysML Xtext agrees (the same prefix, keyword and body, with DependencyDeclaration's body inlined; the inlining is not ported). The rule is the clause as written.

DependencyDeclaration@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.3 states DependencyDeclaration = ( Identification 'from' )? client += [QualifiedName] ( ',' client += [QualifiedName] )* 'to' supplier += [QualifiedName] ( ',' supplier += [QualifiedName] )*. The SysML Xtext has no DependencyDeclaration rule; SysML.xtext's Dependency inlines this body. Cross-references [QualifiedName] are refs to QualifiedName by the derivation's convention. The rule is the clause as written.

Differencing@kerml.decision: As KerML 8.2.4.1.5 states it: the differencing type, as a cross-reference `[QualifiedName]` or as an owned OwnedFeatureChain. The Xtext rule is identical.

DifferencingPart@kerml.decision: As KerML 8.2.4.1.1 states it: 'differences', then one or more Differencing separated by commas. The Xtext fragment is identical. The leading keyword is unique among TypeRelationshipPart's four alternatives in the same clause (`disjoint from`, `unions`, `intersects`, `differences`), so the alternatives do not overlap. TypeDeclaration, in the same clause, repeats relationship parts with `TypeRelationshipPart*`, so the same part may occur more than once. Repeating the keyword and continuing the comma list both accept a further target.

Disjoining@kerml.decision: KerML 8.2.4.1.4 states Disjoining = ( 'disjoining' Identification )? 'disjoint' ( typeDisjoined = [QualifiedName] | typeDisjoined = FeatureChain ) 'from' ( disjoiningType = [QualifiedName] | disjoiningType = FeatureChain ) RelationshipBody. The KerML Xtext writes `Identification?` inside the optional group and OwnedFeatureChain where the clause writes FeatureChain; neither is taken over, since the clause's own reference is FeatureChain. The `{ ownedRelatedElement += ... }` actions are abstract syntax, not syntax. The rule is the clause as written.

DisjoiningPart@kerml.decision: As KerML 8.2.4.1.1 states it: 'disjoint' 'from', then one or more OwnedDisjoining separated by commas. The Xtext fragment is identical. The leading keyword is unique among TypeRelationshipPart's four alternatives in the same clause (`disjoint from`, `unions`, `intersects`, `differences`), so the alternatives do not overlap. TypeDeclaration, in the same clause, repeats relationship parts with `TypeRelationshipPart*`, so the same part may occur more than once. Repeating the keyword and continuing the comma list both accept a further target.

DoActionMember@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.18.1 states DoActionMember : StateSubactionMembership = MemberPrefix kind = 'do' ownedRelatedElement += StateActionUsage. The SysML Xtext writes the keyword as `kind = DoActionKind`, an enum whose literal is 'do'. The rule is the clause as written.

Documentation.decision: As KerML 8.2.3.3.2 and SysML 8.2.2.4.2 both state it, so one shared unit: `doc`, an Identification, an optional `locale` string, and the REGULAR_COMMENT body. The Xtext writes `Identification?`, the same language, because the specification's Identification (KerML 8.2.3.1) is nullable. Unlike Comment, the keyword is required.

EffectBehaviorMember@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.18.3 states `'do' { kind = 'effect' } ownedRelatedElement += EffectBehaviorUsage`. The braced part assigns into the abstract syntax and contributes no token. The Xtext writes `kind = EffectFeatureKind ownedRelatedElement += EffectBehaviorUsage`, and EffectFeatureKind (SysML.xtext:1913) is an enum whose only literal is `effect = 'do'`, so the two accept the same keyword. The 'do' here is the effect of a transition and is not the same 'do' as a state's DoActionMember, which the same clause states separately over StateActionUsage; the two are told apart by where they appear, not by their keyword.

EffectBehaviorUsage@sysml.decision: A transcription of SysML 8.2.2.18.3. The five alternatives are the effect a transition may carry after 'do', and they mirror the five of StateActionUsage with one difference worth keeping in view: the Transition* forms end in `( '{' ActionBodyItem* '}' )?` where the State* forms end in ActionBody, so an effect's body is optional braces rather than a body that may be a ';'. That is why EmptyActionUsage appears here without a ';' after it, unlike in StateActionUsage where the first alternative is `EmptyActionUsage ';'`: a transition effect is followed by the 'then' of its succession, not by a terminator of its own.

ElementFilterMember.decision: A member prefix, `filter`, the condition, and a semicolon. The condition is an OwnedExpression, which is why this production could not be derived until the expression layer was.

ElementReferenceMember.decision: `memberElement = [QualifiedName]`. A Membership whose member is named rather than owned, so the brackets are the whole point: the element is declared elsewhere.

EmptyActionUsage@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.18.1 states this production as `EmptyActionUsage : ActionUsage = {}` — an empty right-hand side. The Xtext says the same thing in its own notation, `{SysML::ActionUsage}`, which is an Xtext action creating an object and consuming nothing. Both therefore derive the empty string, and the rule is an empty sequence. It exists so that a state subaction can be written with no behaviour at all: StateActionUsage's first alternative is `EmptyActionUsage ';'`, which is what makes a bare `entry;` or `do;` a state action whose body is empty, rather than a syntax error. The ';' belongs to that alternative and not to this production, which is why this rule is empty rather than being the terminator itself.

EmptyEndMember@sysml.decision: A transcription of SysML 8.2.2.18.3: `EmptyEndMember : EndFeatureMembership = ownedRelatedElement += EmptyFeature`, where EmptyFeature is `{}`. There is no second opinion to weigh — the pinned pilot grammar has no EmptyEndMember rule, using EmptySourceEndMember in the one place TransitionSuccession needs it — so the clause is the only source. The production contributes no tokens. Its purpose is the source end of a transition succession: `then off` names only a target, and the source is supplied by the transition that owns the succession, so the clause puts an empty end in the position the text leaves unwritten.

EmptyFeature.decision: The clause gives this production the body `{ }`, an action block with no syntax in it: it constructs a Feature and consumes nothing. So it matches the empty string, which is what an empty sequence is.

EmptyMultiplicity@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.9.1 states EmptyMultiplicity : Multiplicity = { }, an action that creates a Multiplicity and consumes no tokens. The SysML Xtext writes {SysML::Multiplicity}, the same. The rule is the empty sequence.

EmptyMultiplicityMember@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.9.1 states EmptyMultiplicityMember : OwningMembership = ownedRelatedElement += EmptyMultiplicity. The SysML Xtext is identical. The rule is the clause as written.

EmptyParameterMember@sysml.decision: A transcription of SysML 8.2.2.17.4. The clause and the Xtext state this production identically — `ownedRelatedElement += EmptyUsage` in both — so there is nothing to weigh. It contributes no tokens: EmptyUsage is `{}`, and the whole point of the production is to occupy a parameter position in the abstract syntax that the concrete syntax leaves unwritten. That is why it appears in rules such as SendNodeDeclaration's SenderReceiverPart, where `send x to y` has no 'via' sender: the clause supplies an empty parameter where the sender would be, so the two spellings of a send action produce the same shape of model.

EmptyUsage@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.17.4 states this production as `EmptyUsage : ReferenceUsage = {}` — an empty right-hand side. The Xtext says the same in its own notation, `{SysML::ReferenceUsage}`, an object-creating action that consumes no input. Both derive the empty string, so the rule is an empty sequence. It is the usage that stands in an EmptyParameterMember, occupying a parameter position the concrete syntax leaves unwritten: it is what lets `send x to y`, which names no sender, build the same shape of model as `send x via s to y`.

EndFeaturePrefix@kerml.decision: An optional `const` and then `end`, as KerML 8.2.4.3.1 states it.

EndUsagePrefix@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.6.2 states EndUsagePrefix : Usage = isEnd ?= 'end' ( ownedRelationship += OwnedCrossFeatureMember )?. The SysML Xtext is identical. Note 1 constrains isConstant on end usages, which is semantics, not syntax. The rule is the clause as written.

EntryActionMember@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.18.1 states EntryActionMember : StateSubactionMembership = MemberPrefix kind = 'entry' ownedRelatedElement += StateActionUsage. The SysML Xtext writes the keyword as `kind = EntryActionKind`, an enum whose literal is 'entry'. The rule is the clause as written.

EntryTransitionMember@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.18.1 states EntryTransitionMember : FeatureMembership : MemberPrefix ( ownedRelatedElement += GuardedTargetSuccession | 'then' ownedRelatedElement += TargetSuccession ) ';', with ':' for '=' in the header (SYSML21-402 item 8). Deviation EntryTransitionMember (follow_xtext) reads TransitionSuccession for TargetSuccession, as the SysML Xtext does; TargetSuccession carries its own 'then' and would double it. The rest is the clause as written.

EnumeratedValue@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.8 states EnumeratedValue : EnumerationUsage = 'enum'? Usage. Deviation EnumeratedValue (follow_xtext) adds the leading UsageExtensionKeyword* the SysML Xtext has and every other usage production carries, which the corpus uses. The Xtext's EnumerationUsageKeyword is 'enum' under a keyword rule and is not ported.

EnumerationBody@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.8 states EnumerationBody : EnumerationDefinition = ';' | '{' ( ownedRelationship += AnnotatingMember | ownedRelationship += EnumerationUsageMember )* '}'. The SysML Xtext uses a `=>` syntactic predicate, which exists to steer the pilot's LL parser and is not ported. The rule is the clause as written.

EnumerationDefinition@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.8 states EnumerationDefinition = DefinitionExtensionKeyword* 'enum' 'def' DefinitionDeclaration EnumerationBody, and the SysML Xtext agrees (the same structure; the keyword pair is factored into a keyword rule, a renaming). The rule is the clause as written.

EnumerationUsage@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.8 states EnumerationUsage : EnumerationUsage = UsagePrefix 'enum' Usage. The SysML Xtext factors the keyword into a keyword rule, a renaming. The rule is the clause as written.

EnumerationUsageMember@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.8 states EnumerationUsageMember : VariantMembership = MemberPrefix ownedRelatedElement += EnumeratedValue. The SysML Xtext is identical. The rule is the clause as written.

EventOccurrenceUsage@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.9.2 states EventOccurrenceUsage = OccurrenceUsagePrefix 'event' ( ownedRelationship += OwnedReferenceSubsetting FeatureSpecializationPart? | 'occurrence' UsageDeclaration? ) UsageCompletion. The SysML Xtext is the same, with 'occurrence' as its OccurrenceUsageKeyword rule. The rule is the clause as written.

ExhibitStateUsage@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.18.2 states ExhibitStateUsage = OccurrenceUsagePrefix 'exhibit' ( ownedRelationship += OwnedReferenceSubsetting FeatureSpecializationPart? | 'state' UsageDeclaration ) ValuePart? StateUsageBody. The SysML Xtext writes UsageDeclaration? and factors 'state' into a keyword rule; UsageDeclaration is already nullable, so neither changes the language. The rule is the clause as written.

ExitActionMember@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.18.1 states ExitActionMember : StateSubactionMembership = MemberPrefix kind = 'exit' ownedRelatedElement += StateActionUsage. The SysML Xtext writes the keyword as `kind = ExitActionKind`, an enum whose literal is 'exit'. The rule is the clause as written.

Expose@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.26.2 puts the 'expose' keyword in this production: `'expose' ( MembershipExpose | NamespaceExpose ) RelationshipBody`, with MembershipExpose = MembershipImport and NamespaceExpose = NamespaceImport. The Xtext omits it here and attaches it inside each branch instead, through the ExposePrefix fragment (SysML.xtext:2366), which spells it as a visibility assignment: `visibility = ExposeVisibilityKind`, an enum whose only literal is `protected = 'expose'` (2370). The same token sequence results either way — 'expose', then an import declaration, then a relationship body — so this is a difference in where the keyword is attached in the abstract syntax, not in the language. The clause's placement is taken. It also keeps the keyword from being stated twice: the branch productions are the import declarations, and nothing in this rule requires them to carry the keyword themselves.

Expression@kerml.decision: A feature prefix, `expr`, an optional declaration, an optional value and a function body. The declaration is OPTIONAL, against the clause as printed and with the Xtext: OMG issue KERML11-181 names this exact clause and states the reference should be optional, so the missing `?` is an acknowledged defect.

ExpressionBody@kerml.decision: Braces around a function body part.

ExpressionBody@sysml.decision: SysML states no ExpressionBody clause; the pack reports none. The SysML reading is fixed by deviation ExpressionBody (follow_xtext): SysML expression bodies read SysML's CalculationBody rather than KerML's '{' FunctionBodyPart '}', decided on corpus lines that put the SysML prefix `ref` inside forAll bodies. The SysML Xtext states exactly that override. The rule is the deviation's reading and nothing more.

ExpressionParameterMember@sysml.decision: A transcription of SysML 8.2.2.17.7. The clause and the Xtext state this production identically — `ownedRelatedElement += OwnedExpression` in both — so there is nothing to weigh. It contributes no tokens; its whole content is a full OwnedExpression, not anything narrower, which is what admits the comparisons and arithmetic that appear as loop and branch conditions. Narrowing it would be the kind of range restriction a parser generator wants and the language does not state.

ExtendedDefinition@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.27 states ExtendedDefinition : Definition = BasicDefinitionPrefix? DefinitionExtensionKeyword+ 'def' Definition, and the SysML Xtext agrees (identical). The rule is the clause as written.

ExtendedUsage@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.27 states ExtendedUsage : Usage = UnextendedUsagePrefix UsageExtensionKeyword+ Usage. The SysML Xtext is identical. The rule is the clause as written.

ExtentExpression.decision: 'all' followed by the type whose extent is taken. Table 6 puts `all` in the highest tier of all, above the unary operators.

Feature@kerml.decision: Two ways to open a feature, then an optional value and a body. The first alternative takes a FeaturePrefix and is announced by either the `feature` keyword or a prefix metadata member, and its declaration is optional — which is what allows an unnamed feature. The second takes an end or basic prefix and requires the declaration, because nothing else would announce it. `ValuePart? TypeBody` applies to both, which is the point the clause text gets wrong.

FeatureBinding@sysml.decision: A transcription of SysML 8.2.2.17.4. The clause and the Xtext state this production identically — `ownedRelatedElement += OwnedExpression` in both — so there is nothing to weigh. It contributes no tokens. Note that it carries no '=' or ':=': this is a FeatureValue bound by position, which is how a node parameter holds an expression without an operator being written, the same device SatisfactionFeatureValue uses after 'by'.

FeatureChain@kerml.decision: One chaining feature, then ONE OR MORE dotted continuations. The repetition is '+' and not '*', so a feature chain has at least two segments by construction: a single name is not a chain.

FeatureChainExpression.decision: An operand, a dot, and the feature being reached. See NonFeatureChainPrimaryArgumentMember for why the left operand is not in fact restricted to non-chains, and what that means for `a.b.c`.

FeatureChainMember@kerml.decision: A feature reference member or an owned feature chain member, as KerML 8.2.5.8.2 states it.

FeatureChainMember@sysml.decision: A qualified name or an owned feature chain member, as SysML 8.2.2.17.5 states it.

FeatureChainPrefix@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.16 states FeatureChainPrefix : Feature = ( ownedRelationship += OwnedFeatureChaining '.' )+ ownedRelationship += OwnedFeatureChaining '.'. The SysML Xtext is identical. The rule is the clause as written.

FeatureDeclaration@kerml.decision: An optional `all`, then an identification with an optional specialization or conjugation part, or one of those parts alone, then any number of relationship parts — as KerML 8.2.4.3.1 states it. It cannot be empty: every alternative needs a name or a part.

FeatureDirection.decision: Three keywords, as both clauses state it: KerML 8.2.4.3.1 and SysML 8.2.2.6.2 print the identical production, so one shared unit serves both languages. The Xtext enum lists the same three literals. `inout` is its own keyword, not `in` followed by `out`: the lexer reads a whole name, so the alternatives cannot be confused.

FeatureElement@kerml.decision: Ten alternatives, in the order KerML 8.2.3.4.3 states them. This is the production that names every kind of feature the language has, and it is the counterpart of NonFeatureElement in the same clause: the two together partition what a member of a namespace can be, once annotating elements are set aside.

FeatureIdentification@kerml.decision: Written as the clause states it: a short name in angle brackets optionally followed by a name, or a name alone. The pilot Xtext has no rule of this name, so there is no second opinion to weigh. The two alternatives do not overlap, since the first begins with '<' and the second with NAME. Short name and name are both the NAME terminal, which covers both the basic and the quoted unrestricted form.

FeatureInverting@kerml.decision: KerML 8.2.4.3.6 states FeatureInverting = ( 'inverting' Identification? )? 'inverse' ( featureInverted = [QualifiedName] | featureInverted = OwnedFeatureChain ) 'of' ( invertingFeature = [QualifiedName] | ownedRelationship += OwnedFeatureChain ) RelationshipBody. The KerML Xtext is the same syntax. The clause writes `Identification?` inside the group here, unlike its siblings; it is kept as written. The rule is the clause as written.

FeatureMember@kerml.decision: Two alternatives, as KerML 8.2.4.1.6 states them. The distinction between them is the `member` keyword that TypeFeatureMember carries and OwnedFeatureMember does not, and that keyword is the whole of the concrete-syntax difference.

FeaturePrefix@kerml.decision: An end prefix with an optional owned cross feature member, or a basic prefix; then any number of prefix metadata members — as KerML 8.2.4.3.1 states it.

FeatureReference.decision: `[QualifiedName]`. The production is nothing but the bracketed name: a FeatureReference is a Feature identified by resolution, not declared here.

FeatureReferenceExpression.decision: A reference to a feature, then the empty result every expression carries.

FeatureRelationshipPart@kerml.decision: Four alternatives, as KerML 8.2.4.3.1 states them, and the Xtext fragment lists the same four in the same order. The alternatives are separated by their leading keywords. ChainingPart begins with 'chains', InvertingPart with 'inverse', and TypeFeaturingPart with 'featured'. TypeRelationshipPart is not stated in this clause, so whether it is also keyword-led is for its own unit to establish. FeatureDeclaration repeats this part with `*`, so relationship parts may follow one another in any order.

FeatureSpecialization.decision: Five alternatives, as KerML 8.2.4.3.1 and SysML 8.2.2.6.5 both state them, so one shared unit. The fourth alternative is Crosses, the production both clauses define as `CROSSES ownedRelationship += OwnedCrossSubsetting`. The Xtext names it Crossings instead. That is the pilot's name for its own rule, not a different construct, and the rule follows the specification's name. Each alternative begins with its own special lexical terminal (TYPED_BY or DEFINED_BY, SUBSETS, REFERENCES, CROSSES, REDEFINES), so the alternatives do not overlap.

FeatureSpecializationPart.decision: As both clauses state it: KerML 8.2.4.3.1 and SysML 8.2.2.6.5 print the same two alternatives, so one shared unit serves both languages. Either at least one specialization comes first, with an optional multiplicity among them, or the multiplicity comes first. The Xtext marks the leading FeatureSpecialization+ with `->`, a syntactic predicate that commits the LL parser to the first alternative. That is a parser-generator workaround and is not ported. Without it the rule is ambiguous when no MultiplicityPart is present, because a run of specializations can split between the leading `+` and the trailing `*` in more than one way. Every split denotes the same list, so the ambiguity is harmless, but a recursive-descent implementation must read specializations greedily, not try each split. Note that this rule, as written, does not derive the empty string: a declaration with no specialization and no multiplicity omits this part through FeatureDeclaration's optionality.

FeatureTyping@kerml.decision: KerML 8.2.4.3.2 states FeatureTyping = ( 'specialization' Identification )? 'typing' typedFeature = [QualifiedName] TYPED_BY GeneralType RelationshipBody. The KerML Xtext writes the optional name part as `( 'specialization' Identification? )?`; the specification's Identification can already be empty, so the inner '?' adds nothing, and references FeatureType where the clause references GeneralType; FeatureType's body is not in this pack, so the clause's reference is kept. TYPED_BY is the special lexical terminal of KerML 8.2.2.7, written out as keyword alternatives. The rule is the clause as written.

FeatureTyping@sysml.decision: As SysML 8.2.2.6.5 states it: an OwnedFeatureTyping or a ConjugatedPortTyping. This is the SysML variant (ADR-0014). ConjugatedPortTyping is not defined in this clause, so whether it overlaps OwnedFeatureTyping is for its own unit to establish. The Xtext rule is identical.

FeatureValue.decision: As KerML 8.2.5.10 and SysML 8.2.2.6.2 both state it, in the same words, so one shared unit. One of three introducers comes first, then an OwnedExpression. The introducers are `=` for a bound value, `:=` for an initial value, and `default` for a default, which may itself be followed by `=` or `:=`. The `{ isInitial }` and `{ isDefault }` assignments set properties and consume no tokens. A bare `default` followed directly by the expression is allowed; the clause makes the operator after it optional. The Xtext rule is the same.

FilterPackage@kerml.decision: As KerML 8.2.3.4.2 states it: an ImportDeclaration, then one or more FilterPackageMembers, each a bracketed OwnedExpression. This is the KerML variant (ADR-0014); the SysML clause states the production differently, which is why it is split. The Xtext writes FilterPackageImport where this clause writes ImportDeclaration. This clause does not define a FilterPackageImport, and the rule follows the clause's ImportDeclaration. The clause's ImportDeclaration makes the rule indirectly recursive: ImportDeclaration includes NamespaceImport, whose second alternative is a FilterPackage. So `a::*[x][y]` can parse as one filter package with two members, or as a filter package nested inside another. The token language is the same either way, since a nested filter package only adds more bracketed members. The Earley oracle accepts the ambiguity; a recursive-descent implementation must choose the flat reading. The clause is followed.

FilterPackage@sysml.decision: As SysML 8.2.2.5.1 states it: a FilterPackageImport, then one or more FilterPackageMembers, each a bracketed OwnedExpression. This is the SysML variant (ADR-0014). The Xtext rule is identical. Note that this clause uses FilterPackageImport without defining it: no `FilterPackageImport =` production appears in 8.2.2.5.1. Its definition, or its absence from the specification, is for FilterPackageImport's own unit to establish.

FilterPackageImport@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.5.1 uses FilterPackageImport and never defines it, an omission OMG has as SYSML21-449. The definition is taken from the specification's Tier B' BNF (SysML-textual-bnf.kebnf line 172): `FilterPackageImport : Import = ImportDeclaration { visibility = 'public' }`. The action sets visibility and consumes no tokens, so syntactically this is an ImportDeclaration. The Xtext writes FilterPackageMembershipImport | FilterPackageNamespaceImport, which accepts the same tokens. Recorded as deviation FilterPackageImport.

FilterPackageMember.decision: As KerML 8.2.3.4.2 and SysML 8.2.2.5.1 both state it, so one shared unit: `[`, an OwnedExpression, `]`. The Xtext writes `visibility = FilterPackageMemberVisibility OwnedExpression ']'`, where FilterPackageMemberVisibility is an enum whose one literal, `private`, is written `'['` (KerML.xtext line 220). That consumes the same `[` and sets the visibility as a side effect. The tokens are identical. The clause's form is followed, and whether a filter member is private is a matter for the abstract syntax.

Flow@kerml.decision: A feature prefix, `flow`, the declaration, and the body. The same four-part shape as BindingConnector and Succession. The declaration is named FlowDeclaration, not ItemFlowDeclaration as the clause's reference says — see the notes.

FlowDeclaration@kerml.decision: KerML 8.2.5.9.2 gives two alternatives. The first is a FeatureDeclaration, an optional ValuePart, an optional `of` payload, and optionally `from` end `to` end. The second is an optional `all`, then end `to` end. The rule makes the FeatureDeclaration in the first alternative optional, which the clause does not. That was a conflict with the Xtext, adjudicated follow_xtext and recorded as deviation FlowDeclaration, explicitly as an extrapolation. KERML11-181 makes declarations optional in Expression productions but does not name Flow. The decision rests on the same shape as those productions, Connector's explicit `FeatureDeclaration?`, and this production's own anonymous second alternative. Note that the same clause's Flow and SuccessionFlow name `ItemFlowDeclaration`, a stale name filed as KERML11-114.

FlowDeclaration@sysml.decision: As SysML 8.2.2.16 states it, with two alternatives. The first is a UsageDeclaration, an optional ValuePart, an optional `of` payload, and optionally `from` end `to` end. The second is end `to` end, with no `all`, unlike KerML. This is the SysML variant (ADR-0014). The Xtext differs in two places, neither changing the language. First, it writes `UsageDeclaration?` where the clause writes `UsageDeclaration`. SysML 8.2.2.6.2 defines UsageDeclaration as `Identification FeatureSpecializationPart?`, and Identification is nullable (SysML 8.2.2.2), so the clause's bare UsageDeclaration already admits the empty case. Second, it writes PayloadFeatureMember where the clause writes FlowPayloadFeatureMember. This clause defines FlowPayloadFeatureMember as a membership over FlowPayloadFeature, and FlowPayloadFeature as PayloadFeature, so the payload is the same PayloadFeature either way.

FlowDefinition@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.16 states FlowDefinition : OccurrenceDefinitionPrefix 'flow' 'def' Definition, and the SysML Xtext agrees (the same structure; the keyword pair is factored into a keyword rule, a renaming). The rule is the clause as written. The clause's header is `FlowDefinition :` with no '=' and no result type; the body that follows is unambiguous and is taken as written.

FlowEnd@kerml.decision: KerML 8.2.5.9.2 states FlowEnd = ( OwnedReferenceSubsetting '.' )? FlowFeatureMember, and the pack notes the clause's malformation is in PayloadFeature, not here. The KerML Xtext instead writes ( FlowEndSubsetting )? with the '.' moved inside a separate rule. That is a refactoring into a rule this production's clause does not name, so it is not ported; the rule is the clause as written.

FlowEnd@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.16 states FlowEnd = ( FlowEndSubsetting )? FlowFeatureMember, with FlowEndSubsetting defined in the same clause, and the SysML Xtext is identical. SysML states it differently from KerML 8.2.5.9.2 (which inlines OwnedReferenceSubsetting '.'), which is why this is its own variant; the rule is SysML's clause as written.

FlowEndMember.decision: A membership wrapping one FlowEnd, with no tokens of its own. KerML 8.2.5.9.2 and SysML 8.2.2.16 state the same body, `ownedRelatedElement += FlowEnd`, so this is one shared unit. The two languages define FlowEnd differently: KerML uses an optional OwnedReferenceSubsetting followed by `.`, SysML an optional FlowEndSubsetting. That difference belongs to FlowEnd. The Xtext rule agrees.

FlowEndSubsetting@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.16 states FlowEndSubsetting : ReferenceSubsetting = referencedFeature = [QualifiedName] | referencedFeature = FeatureChainPrefix. The first alternative lacks the '.' that separates it from the flow feature; deviation FlowEndSubsetting (follow_xtext) adds it, as the SysML Xtext does. The second alternative is the clause as written. The `{ ownedRelatedElement += referencedFeature }` action is abstract syntax.

FlowFeature.decision: KerML 8.2.5.9.2 states FlowFeature : Feature = ownedRelationship += FlowFeatureRedefinition, and SysML 8.2.2.16 states the same body with result ReferenceUsage; the result metaclass is not syntax, so the unit is shared. The KerML Xtext names the referenced rule FlowRedefinition, a renaming. The pack notes the clause's malformation is in PayloadFeature, not here. Note 1 constrains the feature's direction, which is semantics and not grammar.

FlowFeatureMember.decision: KerML 8.2.5.9.2 and SysML 8.2.2.16 both state FlowFeatureMember : FeatureMembership = ownedRelatedElement += FlowFeature, and the KerML Xtext agrees. The pack notes the clause's malformation is in PayloadFeature, not here. The rule is the clause as written.

FlowFeatureRedefinition.decision: KerML 8.2.5.9.2 states FlowFeatureRedefinition : Redefinition = redefinedFeature = [QualifiedName]. SysML 8.2.2.16 states the same body under the misspelled header FlowFeatureRefefinition while referencing FlowFeatureRedefinition; deviation FlowFeatureRedefinition (follow_spec) reads the header as the referenced spelling, so both languages state the same body and the unit is shared. The pilot Xtext has no such rule. A cross-reference [QualifiedName] is a ref to QualifiedName by the derivation's convention.

FlowPayloadFeature@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.16 states FlowPayloadFeature : PayloadFeature = PayloadFeature. The SysML Xtext has no FlowPayloadFeature rule. The result metaclass PayloadFeature and the referenced production PayloadFeature share a name; the body is a reference to the production. The rule is the clause as written.

FlowPayloadFeatureMember@sysml.decision: As SysML 8.2.2.16 states it: a membership wrapping one FlowPayloadFeature, with no tokens of its own. The same clause defines FlowPayloadFeature as PayloadFeature. The pilot SysML Xtext has no rule of this name; it uses PayloadFeatureMember directly, which accepts the same tokens. The clause's production is followed.

FlowUsage@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.16 states FlowUsage = OccurrenceUsagePrefix 'flow' FlowDeclaration DefinitionBody. The SysML Xtext factors the keyword into a keyword rule, a renaming. The rule is the clause as written.

ForLoopNode@sysml.decision: A transcription of SysML 8.2.2.17.7. The clause and the Xtext state this production identically, token for token (SysML.xtext:1624), so there is nothing to weigh. Nothing here is optional: a for loop always declares a variable, always names a sequence after 'in', and always has a body. The variable's own syntax, including its optional type, is inside ForVariableDeclarationMember, and the sequence is a NodeParameterMember, which is what admits a parenthesised literal sequence as readily as a named feature.

ForVariableDeclaration@sysml.decision: A transcription of SysML 8.2.2.17.7: `ForVariableDeclaration : ReferenceUsage = UsageDeclaration`. The clause and the Xtext state it identically, so there is nothing to weigh. The production adds nothing to UsageDeclaration but a metaclass: it exists so that the variable a for loop declares is a ReferenceUsage in the model rather than whatever UsageDeclaration would otherwise produce. Being a wrapper over one production with no tokens of its own is why the clause's own ForVariableDeclarationMember can route around it without changing what parses.

ForVariableDeclarationMember@sysml.decision: Adjudicated. SysML 8.2.2.17.7 states `ownedRelatedElement += UsageDeclaration`, and the rule departs from that literal text; the reasoning is recorded as the deviation ForVariableDeclarationMember, follow_xtext. UsageDeclaration is not an element — the pilot declares it a fragment (SysML.xtext:596), which contributes features to its caller's object rather than instantiating one — so it cannot be the target of a list-valued element assignment. The specification's own text settles which wrapper was meant: the three siblings in this clause each assign an element-producing production, 8.2.2.6.2 states the identical shape in `OwnedCrossFeatureMember` over `OwnedCrossFeature : ReferenceUsage = BasicUsagePrefix UsageDeclaration`, and `ownedRelatedElement += UsageDeclaration` appears in exactly one clause of the whole export, this one. Both readings accept the same text, so this changes no acceptance; it makes the clause's own ForVariableDeclaration reachable instead of orphaned.

ForkNode@sysml.decision: A transcription of SysML 8.2.2.17.3: `ControlNodePrefix isComposite ?= 'fork' UsageDeclaration ActionBody`. The `isComposite ?=` assigns into the abstract syntax and contributes no token. The Xtext's `UsageDeclaration?` is redundant against the clause's `UsageDeclaration`, since UsageDeclaration is nullable through Identification, which is what lets a fork be written bare.

FramedConcernMember@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.21.1 states FramedConcernMember : FramedConcernMembership = MemberPrefix? 'frame' ownedRelatedElement += FramedConcernUsage. The SysML Xtext writes MemberPrefix without the '?' and the keyword as `kind = FramedConcernKind`, an enum whose one literal is 'frame'. The clause writes MemberPrefix?; MemberPrefix is ( visibility = VisibilityIndicator )? and already nullable, so the '?' is kept as written and changes nothing. The rule is the clause as written.

FramedConcernUsage@sysml.decision: SysML 8.2.2.21.1 prints FramedConcernUsage with CalculationBody and an undefined CalculationUsageDeclaration. Deviation FramedConcernUsage (follow_xtext, SYSML21-366, SYSML21-449) reads it with ConstraintUsageDeclaration and RequirementBody, as the SysML Xtext and Tier B' do. The alternatives' structure is the clause's.

Function@kerml.decision: KerML 8.2.5.7.1 states Function = TypePrefix 'function' ClassifierDeclaration FunctionBody. The KerML Xtext is identical. The rule is the clause as written.

FunctionBody@kerml.decision: A semicolon, or braces around a function body part, as KerML 8.2.5.7.1 states it.
